blk_part_02_part_2_thrusters_a_balloon_w.text: A cold-gas thruster is the same idea, made strong and precise. A tank holds gas under high pressure. A valve opens, and the gas rushes out of a nozzle. It is the simplest kind of rocket. Nothing burns, and there is no fuel. The Roadster's thrusters use only compressed air. Spacecraft have used this kind of thruster for decades to make small, exact adjustments.

blk_part_02_part_2_thrusters_a_balloon_w.text: But there is a catch. Cold gas is not very efficient. It is great for short, sharp pushes, but poor for anything that lasts. The car carries about 250 kg of air in its tanks. A rough estimate, not a Tesla figure, says a 1,500 kg car would use about 25 kg of air every second just to stay still in the air. If that estimate is close, the car could hover for seconds, not minutes. So the limited air supply is a big reason why this machine cannot really fly for long, even if it can make powerful jumps.

blk_part_03_part_3_fans_how_a_car_stays_.text: Numbers help here. Engineers measure grip in "G", where 1 G is the pull of gravity. According to engineering vice president Lars Moravy, tyres alone give about 1.26 G. That is good for a fast car, but it does not solve the ceiling problem. Elon Musk said the fans can pull up to 2 G. To stay on a ceiling, the car must be pressed upward harder than gravity pulls it down. A force of 2 G is enough, he said, to hold the car upside down.

blk_part_04_part_4_a_car_built_around_a_.text: If air is the secret, the car must carry a lot of it. The Roadster has 600 litres of compressed air in two carbon-fibre tanks. Tesla said every usable space in the car is filled with these strong, light tanks. Lars Moravy said the air tank can be recharged. In other words, the car is designed around its air supply, almost like a small spacecraft.
